"Preemptive strikes" - meant to "eliminate imminent threats from the Iranian
regime" and prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon.

That's how the US and Israel are attempting to justify their war on Iran - and
if you're only reading Western media, you may take that as fact. But the
reality is, there's nothing preemptive about these strikes, and there's
certainly no legitimate self-defense claim.

International law is clear. Trump's war on Iran is illegal. Here's why:

### **What International Law Says**

Under the UN Charter, states are prohibited from using unilateral force,
except in two cases: (1) when authorized by the UN Security Council or (2) in
self-defense.

The US and Israel did not go to the UN Security Council ahead of Saturday's
strikes on Saturday. That leaves self-defense as the only possible
justification under international law. That justification in this case,
however, falls short when considering the facts.

### **' Israel's Right to Defend Itself'**

Israel contends it would be inadmissible to expect it to wait until Iran is
able to launch a nuclear strike before it is allowed to act in "self-defense."

International law allows states to use force in _anticipatory self-defence_
when an armed attack is underway. If Iran launches a ballistic missile, Israel
does not need to wait for the missile to land to intercept it (interceptive
self-defense). This would be lawful anticipatory self-defense. But
anticipatory self-defense does not permit either preemptive or preventive
strikes.

### **Preemptive Self-Defence**

Preemptive self-defence means that a state considers there is an imminent
threat that another state will use force against it, but has not started its
attack, and decides to preempt it by striking first. In other words, in this
scenario, Israel alleges there is an imminent risk that Iran will attack and
decides to attack first.

The problem is that many states distrust the intentions of other states, not
just Israel. How many states in the Middle East would have cause to strike
Israel preemptively, considering the likelihood of an Israeli attack? In fact,
how do we know that this claimed imminent attack is even real?

According to Reuters, Saturday's attack had been planned for months, and the
exact date had been determined weeks ago, meaning Israel and the US didn't
feel a possible Iranian attack was so imminent that they'd need to strike the
country immediately.

There is some scholarly disagreement as to what the specific boundary between
lawful interception and unlawful pre-emption is. The Global Majority of states
make a strict delimitation: unless the attack is literally underway, use of
force is unlawful. Global North states are more flexible: if the attack is
"imminent" but has not yet started, use of force can be lawful.

Of course, this boils down to what states consider "imminent" to mean.
Theoretically, this test would require that an attack is already being
prepared, even if no offensive weapons have been launched -**** for example,
Poland discovering German preparations for Blitzkrieg days or hours before the
tanks roll out. But because states are likely to abuse any discretion granted
by the law, at some point imminence becomes spurious - i.e., the US claiming
Iraq was planning an "imminent" attack with its "weapons of mass destruction."

This then boils down to evidentiary battles, which is why the Global Majority
objects to pre-emptive force categorically. Evidence can be and often is faked
or kept hidden on account of "national security." Thus, since countries can't
be trusted, Global Majority states prefer to ban the practice altogether. If a
state wants to act preemptively, it should submit its evidence to the UN
Security Council and seek its approval.

If states are allowed to act on "imminent threats" that can't be verified,
then, given existing power inequities, pre-emptive self-defence would simply
be legal cover for realpolitik. Israel would be able to lawfully attack Iran
pre-emptively and at will, but Palestine would not be able to pre-emptively
attack Israel. Might would make right.

### **Preventive Self-Defence**

Preventive self-defence means that a state expects an abstract threat to
materialize in the future, leading to an armed attack against it.

This is the US and Israel's current rationale in Iran, regardless of the term
they use in the media - that Iran _could_ develop nuclear weapons and _might_
use them against Israel, so it is better to be safe than sorry and act
_preventively._

First, there's no evidence Iran was close to developing a nuclear weapon. In
fact, it was only eight months ago that Trump declared, after joining Israel's
12-day war on the country, that Tehran's "key nuclear enrichment facilities
have been completely and totally obliterated." He repeated this claim as late
as last week, during his [State of the Union
address](https://www.npr.org/2026/02/24/nx-s1-5716277/trump-state-union-fact-
check), when he said, the US "obliterated Iran's nuclear weapons program with
an attack on Iranian soil."

Regardless, the preventive self-defense justification is unlawful. States
don't have a blank check to determine who can be a future threat. China can't
preventively invade Taiwan; Russia can't preventively invade Finland.

### **Humanitarian Intervention on Behalf of the Iranian People**

The United States has also argued that it used self-defense against Iran in
defense of the Iranian people to protect them from their government on
humanitarian grounds.

Use of force on humanitarian grounds is not an accepted justification under
international law. Some states have argued in favor of it, like when Belgium
participated in the 1999 NATO bombing campaign against Serbia or when the
United Kingdom responded to Syria's use of chemical weapons in 2018.

Global Majority states have long argued against these "humanitarian
interventions" on the basis that Global North states cannot be trusted to act
for genuinely humanitarian reasons. They point out the lack of intervention in
cases where Western interests were not engaged (Rwanda, 1994) or were aligned
with mass atrocity (Gaza, 2023-present).

In other words, the very concept of humanity is contested: Some peoples are
not seen as human by those with the most power to intervene. Why Iran today
but not Gaza yesterday?

The UN Charter was designed with this in mind. Adolf Hitler, after all,
justified his intervention in Czechoslovakia on the need to protect its German
population. Russia has argued the same in Georgia and Ukraine, and of course,
the US in Iraq and now Iran. None were sincere examples.

If a military power genuinely wishes to use force on humanitarian grounds
without UN authorization, then it should assume the cost of acting unlawfully
in defense of a higher value than the law. Otherwise, this too would become
legal cover for naked realpolitik.

In announcing Saturday's strikes, Trump signaled that his goal is regime
change. He was clear in his message to the Iranian people when [launching the
strikes](https://zeteo.com/p/breaking-us-and-israel-ilegally-attack): "When we
are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take." Iranian
state media later [confirmed](https://apnews.com/article/iran-us-explosion-
tehran-c2f11247d8a66e36929266f2c557a54c) that Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali
Khamenei had been killed in the US-Israeli strikes.

The US and Israel's attack on Iran is unlawful. Media subserviently parroting
the US rationale of a pre-emptive and humanitarian strike are simply failing
to carry out the most basic of fact-checks.

_**Alonso Gurmendi** is an academic researching issues of international law
and international relations from a postcolonial perspective. He works as a
Fellow in Human Rights at the London School of Economics and Political Science
(LSE)._
